# Diagnosing Positive Long Term Fuel Trim in a Ford Fiesta

A persistent positive Long Term Fuel Trim (LTFT) indicates that the Engine Control Unit (ECU) is consistently injecting more fuel than the stoichiometric ratio requires to compensate for a perceived lean condition. In your 2014 Ford Fiesta, the data shows LTFT swinging between 5% and 15% below 2000 RPM before stabilizing at 5% once the engine exceeds that threshold. While an OBD-II scan tool might not report a specific Diagnostic Trouble Code (DTC), the ECU is actively managing the air-fuel mixture, which can lead to poor fuel economy, rough idle, and increased emissions over time.

The most common culprit for a sustained positive LTFT is an unmetered air leak, often referred to as a vacuum leak. When extra air enters the intake manifold after the Mass Air Flow (MAF) sensor, the ECU miscalculates the fuel delivery based on that lower airflow reading. To maintain a stable combustion ratio, the ECU opens the injectors wider than necessary. This adjustment persists as long as the leak exists or if the system cannot return to its original baseline. The fact that your vehicle has run without a thermostat for a year, keeping coolant temperatures at or below 70Â°C, complicates the diagnosis. A cold engine runs richer naturally; however, an ECU that fails to detect the overheating condition might adapt fuel trims aggressively based on oxygen sensor feedback alone, masking other issues until the thermal load changes.

Your observation of the O2 sensors provides critical insight into the system's behavior. The upstream sensor (Bank 1 Sensor 1) is functioning correctly by oscillating between 0V and 0.9V. This "rich-lean" cycling confirms that the catalytic converter is receiving a mixture capable of storing oxygen, meaning the engine isn't so severely lean that it creates a continuous rich bias on its own. The downstream sensor (Bank 1 Sensor 2) reading a steady 0.65V suggests a lean mixture entering the exhaust stream, as this voltage corresponds to a ratio slightly above the stoichiometric point. The occasional dip when releasing the throttle indicates the ECU is momentarily enriching the mixture during deceleration, likely due to the closed-loop control strategy reacting to transient air leaks or changes in vacuum pressure.

To systematically isolate the cause of the instability below 2000 RPM, you must differentiate between a physical leak and an erroneous sensor signal. A propane enrichment test is often the fastest way to confirm a vacuum leak. With the engine idling, introduce a small amount of propane gas into the intake plenum. If the idle RPM rises significantly and the LTFT drops rapidly toward zero or negative values, you have confirmed an unmetered air leak. The ECU interprets this extra fuel demand as a correction to a lean condition, causing it to ramp up the trim percentage until it compensates for the added fuel from the propane.

If the propane test yields no results, the fault likely lies with the airflow measurement itself. Check the Mass Air Flow sensor for contamination or electrical drift. A failing MAF will report less air than is actually present, leading to a lean bias that requires high positive LTFT. Additionally, inspect the intake manifold gaskets and all vacuum lines for cracks or disconnections. The instability below 2000 RPM is typical because low RPM operation relies heavily on manifold vacuum; any leak becomes proportionally larger at lower pressures, causing the trim to swing wildly before the throttle opens enough at higher RPMs to stabilize the pressure dynamics.

Finally, consider the coolant temperature sensor circuit. If the ECU believes the engine is running cooler than it actually is because of the faulty thermostat situation, it may default to a richer fuel map. However, since you are seeing a lean bias requiring correction, the primary issue remains an air-fuel imbalance rather than a thermal mapping error. Addressing the vacuum integrity and verifying MAF accuracy will likely resolve the positive LTFT and restore proper engine performance.
